sentences.t: In August of 1590, a man named John White stepped onto the beach at Roanoke Island, off the coast of what is now North Carolina.
He'd been gone for three years.
He had left behind more than a hundred English settlers, including his own daughter and his infant granddaughter.
And when he walked up to the settlement, there was no one there.
No bodies, no graves, no sign of a fight.
Just a palisade, some scattered belongings, and one word carved into a wooden post.
Croatoan.
So, what actually happened to the Lost Colony?
To answer that, we have to go back a few years, because Roanoke wasn't one attempt, it was three.
The first expedition, in 1584, was basically a scouting trip.
Two ships, sent by Sir Walter Raleigh, landed on the Outer Banks, met the local Algonquian peoples, and came home with glowing reports.
They brought two men back to England with them, Manteo and Wanchese, and that detail matters later.
The second attempt, in 1585, was a military outpost.
About a hundred men under Ralph Lane built a fort on Roanoke Island.
And frankly, it went badly.
They depended on the local tribes for food, relations broke down, and Lane's men killed a Secotan leader named Wingina.
When Francis Drake's fleet stopped by in 1586, the whole garrison begged for a ride home.
Which brings us to the third attempt, the one we actually call the Lost Colony.
In 1587, about a hundred and fifteen settlers sailed from England, and this time it was families, men, women, and children.
They were supposed to settle further north, near the Chesapeake Bay.
But the ship's pilot, a man named Simon Fernandes, refused to take them any further than Roanoke.
Historians still argue about why, but the result was that they were dropped in exactly the place where the English were least welcome.
A few weeks after they landed, John White's daughter, Eleanor Dare, gave birth to a girl named Virginia.
She was the first English child born in the Americas.
And within a month, the colonists persuaded White to sail back to England for supplies.
He planned to be gone a few months.
Then the Spanish Armada happened.
Every ship that could fight was held in England, and White couldn't get back across the Atlantic until 1590.
Before he left, he'd arranged a simple code with the settlers.
If they moved, they were to carve where they had gone.
And if they left in distress, they were to carve a cross above it.
When he found Croatoan carved on that post, there was no cross.

It was the name of an island about fifty miles to the south, today part of Hatteras, and the name of the people who lived there.
Remember Manteo, one of the two men who went to England in 1584?
He was Croatoan.
White wanted to sail there, but a storm hit, his ship was damaged, and the captain turned for home.
He never saw Roanoke, or his family, again.
For centuries, that was where the trail went cold.
But in the last fifteen years, archaeologists working on Hatteras have found English artifacts mixed into Croatoan village sites, a sword hilt, a slate with writing on it, pieces of a gun.
Another team, inland on the mainland, found English pottery at a site some think was a second settlement.
The most likely answer is also the least dramatic.
The colonists didn't vanish.
They split up, moved in with their neighbors, and over a generation or two, they simply became part of them.
Which, honestly, is exactly what John White's carving told us in the first place.
